title: Qsyn A Developer-Friendly Quantum Circuit Synthesis Framework for NISQ Era and Beyond

predicted_errors.error_location: Table I ("COMPARISON WITH PYZX [1] ON THE GATE-LEVEL SYNTHESIS STAGE")
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper states "In Table I, we performed gate-level synthesis to examine the run time and memory usage of Qsyn against PyZX" and then makes detailed numerical claims (shorter runtimes, lower memory, TLE/MLE for PyZX on gf2^128, hwb12, urf4, smaller or equal RZ-counts, shallower circuits on average), but the table contains only a caption and unit line with no data rows. None of the reported results can be verified against the referenced table.

predicted_errors.error_location: Results section / Abstract ("fair comparisons with PyZX")
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract claims "We demonstrate Qsyn's superior performance through fair comparisons with PyZX", yet the comparison is a single-baseline runtime/memory benchmark between a compiled C++ tool and a Python library, with no description of hardware, time/memory limits, benchmark selection, or repetitions. Calling this a 'fair comparison' and concluding superior performance overstates what the (unshown) evidence can support.

The abstract asserts Qsyn "is more developer-friendly than other modern QCS frameworks" and claims a rigorous development flow with "regression testing, continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines, and code linting". The body never presents any evidence, measurement, or even description of these QA practices, nor any comparison of developer-friendliness with other frameworks (Qiskit, t|ket>, Cirq, etc.). The central claim of the paper is therefore unsupported by the reported evidence.

predicted_errors.error_location: Results section, sentence beginning "Compared to PyZX, Qsyn tended to optimize circuits with shorter program runtimes..."
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The same sentence states PyZX encounters TLE and/or MLE on gf2^128, hwb12 and urf4. For those benchmarks no PyZX runtime/memory/gate-count data exist, so the claims that Qsyn had "shorter program runtimes and lower memory usage" and "either smaller or equal RZ-counts" cannot logically include these circuits; the aggregate comparison (including the "on average, shallower circuits" statistic) is computed over an ill-defined, partially missing baseline.

predicted_errors.error_location: Results section, "This is attributed to Qsyn's integration of ZX-calculus and Tableau combined methods"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: A causal attribution of the gate-count/depth improvement to the ZX+Tableau combination is made without any ablation or controlled experiment isolating that feature from the other stated differences (compact MCT ZX representation, early-stopping, improved gadget-removal extraction). The conclusion is not supported by the described experiment.

predicted_errors.error_location: Methods section, "...avoid producing redundant graph complexity [11]" and reference list
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper cites references [1] and [11], but no bibliography is provided, so neither citation can be verified; moreover citing [11] for Qsyn's own claimed algorithmic revisions (compact MCT representation and early-stopping) is ambiguous attribution — it is unclear whether the contribution is the authors' or prior work's.

The only baseline is PyZX, a Python research library, although the paper positions Qsyn against "other modern QCS frameworks". Omitting standard, performance-oriented baselines (e.g., Qiskit, t|ket>, Quartz) makes the comparison inadequate to support the general superiority claim, and no experimental protocol (platform, limits, number of runs) is reported.

The identical funding statement "This work is supported by the National Science and Technology Council R.O.C., Project No.: NSTC 113-2119-M-002-024" is duplicated verbatim (with inconsistent punctuation of the agency name) in two separate footnotes, indicating a production/consistency error in the manuscript.
